title: 100% Death Proof: Stuntman’s Chevy Nova Weaponizes Muscle

body_markdown:
Buddy Joe, 83, exits a white Toyota Tacoma pickup attached to a rented trailer. Medium height, medium build, fit for a guy his age. When he takes off his thick, stylish black sunglasses, he reveals one of those Hollywood faces—you don’t recognize him, per se, but you’ve probably seen frames of him in dozens of movies. His wife, Gayle Hooker, and son, Kanan, pile out of the truck in his wake.


In the rented trailer sits The Jesus, a 1970 Chevrolet Nova. If you’re a movie buff, you might think it’s been done up to look like the car from the 2007 flick *Death Proof* —all scarred and tough and the right kind of ratty, hood brandishing a skull graphic with lightning bolts in place of crossbones. The stunt cage, thick steel bars and gaudy welds exposed, is visible through the windows. You’d almost be right. In fact, this is no mock-up—it’s an actual stunt car from the movie, and Buddy Joe is the actual stuntman who drove it for the cameras.


*Welcome to the[Hagerty Movies and Cars Celebration](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/welcome-to-the-hagerty-movies-and-cars-celebration/) , where we highlight and explore the relationship between[cars and the silver screen](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/movies-and-cars/) .*


**Meet Buddy Joe Hooker.** A stunt veteran whose job it is to be death-proof. First a cowboy and then a gymnast, Buddy Joe followed his father into the stunt business at 13. He has jumped motorcycles, flipped cars, fallen from great heights, and been set on fire. He is an original member of Hollywood’s elite stunt club,[Stunts Unlimited](https://stuntsunlimited.com/) .


James Lipman


*Death Proof,* written and directed by Quentin Tarantino, is about a stunt driver and serial killer (Stuntman Mike, played by Kurt Russell) who stalks and murders women with cars. In the first half of the movie, the Nova is his weapon of choice. It’s a twisted, grotesque film—even by the standards of the man who imagined the fight scenes in *Kill Bill* —but the specific intent with *Death Proof* is to pay homage to the sordid genre of ’60s and ’70s B movies. Tarantino is obsessed with arcane film history, and he sweats minute details to properly honor his cinematic heroes. Naturally, for *Death Proof* , a production about stuntpeople driving cars to the brink of destruction, Tarantino insisted on two points: 1) an all-star team of Hollywood stunt legends and 2) entirely practical stunts, without the use of special effects or CGI. In his words: “real cars, real sh*t, at full… speed.”


On the first point, Tarantino hand-selected Buddy Joe Hooker to be *Death Proof* ’s principal stunt driver and double for Kurt Russell. Buddy Joe’s IMDB page as a stunt performer and coordinator includes highlights like *Close Encounters of the Third Kind, To Live and Die in L.A., Scarface, Harold and Maude, Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Days of Thunder* , the 2000 remake of *Gone in 60 Seconds* , and dozens more. For a sense of the man, consider that his father ran a ranch that provided horses for Westerns; Buddy Joe got his start as a child, doing stunts with horses. As an adult, he jumped a motorcycle over the spinning blades of a landing helicopter ( *Daredevils* ), rolled a truck 17 consecutive times down a sand embankment ( *Clay Pigeon* ), and jumped a car about 120 feet over Burt Reynolds’ head into the Arkansas River ( *White Lightning* ).


The stunt community is familial and close-knit. Which makes sense, given that lives are constantly on the line.


James Lipman


*Death Proof* was a commercial and critical flop. (Roger Ebert, in his 2.5-star review, borrowed from another famous critic to pan Tarantino for “trying to shove art up into the crevices of dreck.”) But it made a lasting impression on me, at the time a car-obsessed teenager. It also seemed to stick with Hooker, the stuntman doubling for an actor playing a fictional stuntman. Maybe that’s why he took a liking to the Nova.


“I usually don’t get attached to cars on set, but from the start, this one just worked well for me,” he says, with a hand laid affectionately on the roof.


Stunt drivers are a photographer’s delight. No matter what we asked Kanan to do with his car for the camera, he executed it without apparent effort.


James Lipman


Production bought and prepped three Novas for the film: one for close-ups and two for stunts. While most stunt cars are prepped in such a way as to hide their safety cages, camera mounts, and general ruggedness, Stuntman Mike’s black Nova is presented as the genuine article in the film. One of them, nicknamed The Jesus on set, became Hooker’s favorite. “The Jesus had a 350 V-8 stroked to 383, with long-tube headers and a four-barrel carburetor. It had good power and it handled better than the others,” Hooker says. He kept an eye on it during production.


“There was an instinct to save it, so before any of the big action sequences, I’d park it a little way’s away,” he explains with a hearty laugh.


James Lipman


The Nova’s rear traction bars are true to ’70s drag cars. But Death Proof’s production crew fitted them mostly because they look badass.


James Lipman


The other prepped car, The Cleetus, was destroyed in one of the film’s major action scenes via a maneuver called a “cannon roll.” At a precise moment and speed, the stunt driver activates a device that fires underneath the car and launches it into the air at an angle, kicking off a series of horizontal rolls that looks astonishing on camera. In *Death Proof* , the scene depicts a ferocious, intentional head-on collision with another car containing Stuntman Mike’s prey.


“Right here,” Buddy Joe says, crouching slightly to jab his finger under the Nova’s rocker sill, just in front of the passenger-side rear tire, “is where we mount the metal tube. In there, we pack a section of telephone pole and some black powder.” Buddy Joe, a magnetic and animated storyteller, has rendered photographer James Lipman and me speechless as we hang on his every word. “Gunpowder, really. When it’s time, and everything’s set up right, I hit the button and the pole blasts out toward the ground, splintering into pieces and sending the car up.”


“You hit the button? Aren’t you… driving?” “Well, yeah,” he says, gesturing with an imaginary helm held out in front of him. “Some guys like to hold it out there with one hand, but I like to keep both hands on the wheel. So I tape the detonator to my thumb.”


For the *Death Proof* cannon roll, Buddy Joe rolled The Cleetus about 160 yards. As it ended, the car slid heinously on its roof in a tempest of screeching metal. He nailed it on the first take, though, and the car stopped almost right in front of the camera. That meant The Jesus was spared, and at the end of production Buddy Joe asked Tarantino if he could have the car. Mostly as a formality, the director sold it to Buddy Joe for about $500.


Though the Nova’s scenes were filmed in Austin, Texas, bringing it to the Santa Ynez Valley, where the movie’s famous Challenger/Charger duel plays, felt right.


Courtesy Dimension Films


> The car slid heinously on its roof in a tempest of screeching metal… He nailed it on the first take.


Buddy Joe’s teenage twin sons, Kanan and Houston, tinkered with The Jesus and drove it to high school near The Snake, a famously twisty section of L.A.’s Mulholland Drive. This was a well-thrashed Hollywood movie car, so the brothers had to refresh a lot of the engine components. They added steel inner panels for the doors, where they were previously exposed to minimize weight and the chance of dangerous projectiles. Out went the Plexiglas barrier between passenger and driver, as well as the tractor seat where actress Rose McGowan sat. (Her character, unsecured and locked inside the crash box, is murdered when Stuntman Mike stands on the brakes at high speed.) A normal seat made a lot more sense for a couple of teens trying to score dates.


The Hookers worked on the brakes, too. During filming, the pedal had been set up to brake only the front axle; a separate pedal was installed near the dead pedal to control the rear brakes—ideal for spinning the car and executing 180s. “We kept it in there for a little bit,” Kanan said, “but it was only because we wanted to mess around. It’s not conducive to much else, though, least of all daily driving.” They returned it to stock aside from a bigger brake booster from a C/K-series truck.


Inner door panels were one of the only additions the Hookers made since the Nova’s days on set.


James Lipman


Kanan—33, clean-cut, meticulous, and crazy about cars—is now out of the stunt business and working for an off-road mapping technology start-up called onX Offroad based out of Montana. He flew home to California to be with us for the shoot, which we staged near Buellton, in the Santa Ynez Valley northwest of Santa Barbara, where the second half of *Death Proof* was shot. “Reuniting with this car is kind of like going back to my childhood, honestly,” he said.


“I’ve always been a gearhead but haven’t done much wrenching since moving away. Getting the Nova sorted for today was super nostalgic.”


Most adults would be horrified to arm their teenage sons with 400–425 horsepower of Detroit muscle in a car never equipped with airbags. Most mothers, though, haven’t stunt doubled for Uma Thurman. “They were born with their father’s DNA,” Gayle says, “and that natural sense of space and time and movement and body awareness.” Both Gayle and Buddy Joe had watched Kanan’s and Houston’s driving skills develop over the years, a process that included karting and training with friends in the professional stunt world. She looks over at Kanan in the still-adoring way a loving mom regards her adult son. He has unloaded the Nova from the trailer and is busy under the hood checking the coolant level. “He’s also in tune with cars. They talk to him.”


Beyond all that, Buddy Joe had the confidence the car would be safe in a crash. After all, that’s what it was built to withstand, to protect the driver. “Once Kanan was strapped in there, I knew he was pretty bulletproof. Might be something that happened to someone else, of course…” he trails off, throwing an animated wink for good measure.


> The Nova is a treasured family car, one they can’t think about ever selling.


Buddy Joe, Gayle, and Kanan. The Hookers are bonded with the car they call “Death Proof.”


James Lipman


***


A beautiful aspect of film is the way your imagination fills in the gap between reality and the on-screen fantasy. Driving a movie car in real life, like meeting any hero, comes with a risk: closing that gap, washing over it with real, finite experiences.


When I make my way up to the matte-black Nova, a bead of sweat trickles down the back of my neck. For a moment, I remember the gore and terror wrought by this car in the film, and I am unsettled.
Kanan is waiting there for me, key and steering wheel in hand. His T-shirt, emblazoned with the Nova’s skull and lightning logo, reads: STUNTMAN MIKE’S PROFESSIONAL DRIVING SCHOOL.


“You ready?” he asks.


> A beautiful aspect of film is the way your imagination fills in the gap between reailty and the on-screen fantasy.


Kanan opens the door and explains how to get into the driver’s seat. Remember, there’s a roll cage to contend with, including a bar that runs horizontally just inside the door. I throw one leg over the thick steel, ducking my head so that it clears the top of the window frame. Using my left hand to hold on to another metal bar, this one wrapped in zip-tied pool-noodle foam and running on the underside of the roof, I not-so-deftly lower myself into the fixed bucket seat. As I swing my other leg—still dangling out of the window—into the car, Kanan warns me to do it slowly. People tend to whack the turn signal at this stage, which is a delicate piece that can easily break off.


The five-point safety harness, set up in both passenger and driver seats, is no joke. Once I’m strapped and buckled in, my position is utterly fixed. The rest of the Nova’s interior is similarly unforgiving—everything unnecessary has been stripped out, including the dashboard and rear seat. In place of the headliner is a drilled steel panel designed to reinforce the roof structure; vehicle coordinators were concerned that the huge upside-down slide might wear through the factory sheetmetal.


If the Nova was parked anywhere in Los Angeles, Kanan would carry the steering wheel around in his backpack, rather than lock the doors.


James Lipman


Mounted above the hub for the quick-release steering wheel are three gauges, which Kanan says were probably bought off the shelf at the local auto parts store. In the middle is the largest readout, the speedometer, flanked by oil pressure and water temperature gauges. The tachometer hangs from a metal bracket on the upper corner of the windshield. A loose tangle of wires curls, exposed, underneath the steering column.


Kanan passes the steering wheel to me through the open window. I slide it onto the hub and carefully but firmly smack it with the fleshy base of my palm. The satisfying click tells me it’s secured, but I pull on it to make sure. Quiet on set. Roll sound. Roll camera. Frame. Action!


James Lipman


I twist the key and the boisterous 383 V-8 fires up, bristling at first but soon settling down into a steady idle. Even amid that din, the interior’s rumbles and rattles are discernible. (You don’t really appreciate what sound deadening does until you spend time in a car that doesn’t have any.) The clangorous cabin was in a lot of ways a feature, not a bug. Tarantino wanted everything real for *Death Proof* , not merely the driving. That meant real noises from the cockpit, real engine note, real click from the automatic gear lever sliding from park to drive.


The metal B&M shift handle is sizzling to the touch from sitting out in the California sun. I shift the GM four-speed automatic with an overdrive into D and the Nova crawls along, seemingly content. Poking my head out the window, I ask Buddy Joe about the gearbox. “I always preferred, as a stuntperson, an automatic—you are much more free to make a car do things,” he explains before twice tapping the Chevy’s roof.


On-command burnout capability is table stakes for a Hollywood stunt car.


James Lipman


On an open stretch of road, I summon a healthy dose of throttle. The Nova roasts its tires without effort through first and second gear. I glance at the rearview mirror to admire the wisps of smoke in my wake. Steering is vague and imprecise on-center, but after a few degrees of input, the truck-spec power assist kicks in and the front end starts catching up with your hands. From there, it’s easy, finger-light adjustment, and at speed, it tracks spear straight. Braking requires a firm stomp before the drums bite down, so I learn to keep a healthy distance to the car in front of me.


The engine delivers reliable grunt and burbles sweetly from its dual Flowmaster exhaust, but a small-block Chevy like this is relatively standard fare in the world of modified V-8s; the secret sauce here is how little the Nova weighs. Stock Novas weighed a hair over 3000 pounds and packed easily tunable engines, which is a big reason why V-8 versions were such popular street racers. (Their anodyne styling was another; in 1969, *Hot Rod* magazine lauded the Nova SS 396’s “total lack of identification” and declared “the sleeper car era has returned.”) With the naked interior and the gas tank gone in favor of a 10-gallon fuel cell, the *Death Proof* Nova clocks in closer to 2800 pounds.


James Lipman


That lack of mass on the rear axle makes the Nova tricky to drive on winding roads. The suspension is unmodified aside from sweet-looking rear traction bars (an old drag racer piece of kit), which means plenty of typical 1970s weight transfer that can sneak up on you if, say, the transmission shifts at the wrong time. Kanan, sitting shotgun, advises me not to overload the front tires and to left-foot brake into corners rather than suddenly lifting off the gas, which can induce an unexpected slide with steering applied.


Despite all that, this is a friendly machine—nothing like its on-screen persona. I understand why Buddy Joe warmed to it on set. As I gaze out over the hood, the skull graphic and the angry duck ornament point the way like they’re on the prow of a devil-may-care pirate ship.


James Lipman


> The skull graphic and the angry duck ornament point the way like they’re on the prow of a devil-may-care pirate ship.


For a minute, I feel like a badass. That is, until I imagine what it would be like to intentionally launch this car into the air, at 60-plus mph, and flip several times before landing upside-down. The spectacle on screen is extraordinary, but being this close to it makes Buddy Joe seem superhuman. Later, someone asks him if stuntpeople have a death wish. He doesn’t hesitate to respond.


“People ask me that, but no, no, I have a life wish. A survival wish. At no point in my career did I ever do anything, ever, that I thought would kill me. It was all about preparation.”


His wife, Gayle, echoes that perspective. “Everybody is working together for a production, and if there’s one weak link, just one, it’s disastrous. Weeks and weeks of planning happen in anticipation of just a few seconds of action. And despite sensing the risks, stuntpeople and coordinators manage to maintain an element of levity.”


***


James Lipman


Kanan and I switch seats. He takes me to a particular section of country road, situated right at the high point of a large field and at the base of some hillsides. I recognize it as the location of *Death Proof* ’s final chase sequence. At high speed, a ’69 Charger and the ’70 Challenger smash into each other repeatedly on these roads, the latter with stuntwoman Zoë Bell (playing herself in the film) frequently strapped to the hood of the car.


Buddy Joe stands on the shoulder, red-tailed hawks soaring overhead, and stares off into the distance toward a dirt road running down the hillside. He doesn’t break concentration. I can tell that a memory is playing in his mind’s eye.


“That whole chase was, for me, among the more nerve-wracking parts of the movie,” he says. “I was in the black Charger, so I had a lot of steel around me. My stress of working with what we were doing was considerably less than stunt driver Tracy Keehn-Dashnaw’s, who had Zoë lying on the hood of the Challenger to consider. Zoë’s only safety was a cable, which was fine, but there were parts of the movie where Quentin wanted me to come alongside of them and whack them. These are old cars! \[Stunt/prep/vehicles department\] did the best they could with them, but you don’t know when an axle is going to break, or a wheel. We even had a couple of those, but it didn’t cause any problems other than some shooting time.”


Buddy Joe was somewhat reluctant to perform take after take of these rear-end rams and sidelong smashes, but Tarantino kept asking. “I just didn’t have it in me to hit that car as hard as he wanted because if something would have happened and I buckled a front wheel on that, the car would flip.”


Every time Buddy Joe would slam into the Challenger, an effects guy lying in the back seat of the car would belay out the cable attached to Bell’s harness via pulleys routed through the hood, amplifying the appearance that she was being flung around. “She could swivel around and make her legs flail right after I hit her. She did an incredible acting job making it look like I hit her way harder than I did. And she never said a word, unless it was something like ‘Can you f***ing go and hit us any harder than that? I didn’t even feel it!’”


A very early piece of *Death Proof* concept art, featuring Mickey Rourke and a Camaro. Familiar flavor, different casting.


James Lipman


He also gives full credit to Keehn-Dashnaw, his counterpart behind the wheel. “She’s one of the better drivers I’ve ever worked with. We gauged everything on when Quentin would say, ‘Hey, can you guys go faster? I need you to do it faster and hit harder.’ We kind of had a mindset where I knew exactly what she was going to do before she did it, and she knew exactly what I was going to do.”


For the climactic final crash, Buddy Joe in the Charger had to come down the lower road at a steady speed so that, when the Challenger came barreling down the ridge, Keehn-Dashnaw could time the violent crash to happen at a precise location in view of the camera car.


“We were going down this way pretty fast, and the road was kind of wet right where I hit her,” Buddy Joe recounts, matter-of-factly, the way you might describe what you did last weekend. “We both spun out, and that wasn’t supposed to happen. But Quentin loved it and said, ‘OK, let’s set the cameras for that instead and go back and do that again.’ So now we’ve got to recreate this maneuver that was initially an accident.”


They got it done, and the scene is absolutely thrilling.


Tarantino flips the bird.


James Lipman


Ribbing each other all while rolling with the punches and remaining professional—that comes with the territory in stunts. Stunt drivers don’t get the glory; they’re not household names. They don’t show up on Jimmy Fallon and laugh at his jokes for YouTube clips. They’re sleepers, and they get the call when CGI won’t cut it.


Buddy Joe, Kanan, and Gayle are standing by the Nova on the side of the road, laughing, teasing, reminiscing. For me, the car is a celebrity, the villain’s trademark tool in the louche, edgy kind of movie you watch with your friends when you’re 16. For them, the Nova is grounded in the real—a treasured family car, one they can’t think about ever selling. Kanan and Gayle were guests on set during the *Death Proof* shoot, and the experience is fixed in their memories. “The car started representing how the boys got to see so much of what their dad did,” Gayle tells me. “Later, for a school project, they made a movie where the Nova is their protector, watching out for them.”


A baleful, matte-black paint job says a lot about *Death Proof’* s Chevy: villainous, all business, and not to be trifled with.


James Lipman


Since driving the Nova, I’ve rewatched *Death Proof* . In the parlance of our times, it hits different now. Some of the mystery is gone, the illusion broken. My sense of wonder remains, though—wonder at the stunt drivers, at all the fascinating little nuances of the car and details about the movie I now possess. There’s less for me to imagine, sure. But I can’t imagine that the badass *Death Proof* Nova could have found a more worthy home than with the Hookers.
